newsitem.title: UK: Australian bonds still attractive for overseas investors.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds still attractive for overseas investors.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries hold the most promise for investors seeking returns within the dollar bloc but Australia is also attractive, analysts said on Tuesday.

In the U.S. the market has a chance to stabilise with further interest rate rises mostly priced in, while Australian bonds are well supported by export commodity prices which are helping to maintain a stable currency, they said.
"Of all these dollar markets the U.S. looks the most solid," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking. "And if I wanted diversification then I would chose Australia."
Within U.S. Treasuries, the five-year area was particularly attractive, he said, with the spread between five- and 30-year paper at around only 30 basis points.
"There is not a lot of protection from things going wrong in the 30-year, and by the same token the five-year sector seems to have most of the bad news built into it," Lewis said.
By 1252 GMT, five-year T-notes were trading at 99-17 to yield 6.74 percent, while the long bond was at 94-07 to yield 7.09 percent.
Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London, said for now U.S. Treasuries were safer than Canadian bonds.

"Treasuries are already priced for about 100 basis points of interest rate increases over the next year and we have seen a fairly solid recovery over the past day or so," he said. "So from a foreign investor's perspective, U.S. dollar assets are probably perferred."
Chester said with the prospect of further U.S. interest rate rises, the Bank of Canada could only afford to wait so long without responding if it wanted to prevent a significant run on its currency.

The Canadian dollar touched a "post-Quebec referendum" peak at 139.95 after the U.S. payrolls figures last Friday, but he noted the U.S. retail sales numbers were due at the end of the week and the U.S. dollar was looking very strong.

"If the Canadian dollar does come under further pressure, the Bank of Canada will step in with a 25 basis point rate increase," he said. "It is difficult to make a persuasive bullish case for (Canadian bonds) at the moment until the Bank of Canada make it known just what they are going to do."
Elizabeth Afseth, in bond sales at Williams de Broe in London, agreed Canadian bonds were struggling under the shadow of a probable rate increase.

"I would be rather careful of the Canadian market," she said. "It has come back a bit and is level with the U.S. on the 10-year at the moment but I don't think we are going to see it trade through very much."
She said U.S. Treasuries offered reasonable value but recommended investors also look at Australian bonds.

Lewis said because Australian and New Zealand dollars were less closely linked to the U.S. than Canadian debt, their respective domestic situations were at least as powerful an influence on how they performed as the U.S. dollar.
"In Australia the worry is that commodity prices could fall," said Lewis.
But although since the beginning of the year there has been a decline in the prices of raw materials, such items as iron ore and coal had held their value well to the benefit of Australia.
"So long as that persists, the currency should be fairly stable and that probably means there won't be any pressure on the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise interest rates," he said.
Lewis said the sharpness of the Australian yield curve, with around 200 basis points spread between money rates and 10-year bonds, meant there was some room for long yields to edge lower.
